newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Jailed Colombian drug lords have comforts of home.
newsitem.headline: Jailed Colombian drug lords have comforts of home.

text.p: The Cali cartel kingpins who U.S. officials say once controlled up to 80 percent of the world cocaine trade, have all the comforts of home as they do their time in Bogota's La Picota prison -- conjugal visits, fine dining, billiards, fresh-cut flowers and, of course, cable.

Brothers Gilberto and Miguel Rodriguez Orejuela were arrested separately in June and August of last year during a nationwide sweep targeting their drug empire. Colombia has refused to extradite them to the United States, and they could be freed in as little as seven years.

The brothers, both reputed billionaires whose extradition is sought by the United States, were kept locked up in their cells on Thursday when a group of foreign journalists was given a rare tour of the maximum-security wing of La Picota.

But comments by the prison's directors about their daily routine, and the trappings of luxury seen inside the prison, would lead anyone to conclude that Colombia's most notorious criminals are not exactly serving "hard time."

Miguel, who is studying business administration and English inside La Picota, also runs a small but well-stocked shop he set up in the prison yard in a brightly painted kiosk decorated with fresh roses named "Poor Miguel's Store."

The vast array of items he dispenses from inside range anywhere from Belgian chocolates and English tea biscuits to Gummi Bears, Power Rangers, Matchbox toy cars and children's walkie talkies. Sanitary napkins, which a guard said were a hot item during three-hour conjugal visits every Wednesday, were also on display in the store where Miguel serves Pepsi and coffee but not Coke.

Miguel and Gilberto share Cellblock B of La Picota with a total of 11 other inmates, including their younger brother, Jorge Elicer, and two other members of the cartel leadership. Another cartel leader, Jorge Santacruz Londono, fled the prison in broad daylight in January and was gunned down by police in early March.

The kitchen and dining room are open all day -- from 6:30 a.m. till lockup at 9 p.m. Breakfast is served till 10:30, inmates can bring in any food they like from the outside and daily newspapers are delivered every morning. Among all the homey touches, a Chinese cellmate occasionally wips up an exotic oriental meal.

When inmates aren't busy studying, or playing mini-soccer or billiards in the prison yard, they can while away the time watching cable TV on sets with screens of up to 19 inches (48 cm) in each of their cells or simply smell the fresh-cut flowers placed in prison corridors.

National Police Col. Hector Escamilla, La Picota's director, declined to comment when asked about U.S. charges that the Rodriguez Orejuelas continue to run their criminal drug syndicate from inside prison. He denied published reports that inmates have open access to cellular phones, but said it was "very difficult" to curb illicit business activity if it was conducted over a public telephone inside the prison that all inmates have a right to use.
They also have open communications with the outside world through day-long visitor sessions on Saturday and Sunday, and unrestricted access to their lawyers.

Judicial sources have said the Rodriguez Orejuelas -- who have been accused of providing millions of dollars in financing for President Ernesto Samper's electoral campaign -- will probably be sentenced to no more than eight to 12 years in prison because of plea bargaining agreements and Colombia's lenient penalties for drug trafficking. Discounting time already served, both could walk free in as little as seven years.

U.S. Attorney General Janet Reno requested the brothers' extradition to the United States in June. But Foreign Minister Maria Emma Mejia reiterated the government's denial of the request in a formal statement to Colombia's Justice Ministry on Thursday, saying that a consitutional ban on extradition passed by Colombia's Congress in 1991 took legal precedence over a 1979 U.S.-Colombia extradition treaty.
